title: Overlap sessions + stalled-chunks + streaming timeouts — product walkthrough
summary: Demo focused on pathological edge cases: overlapping long-lived sessions that create KV cache churn, stalled chunk streaming causing client-side timeouts, and how Redwood routes and degrades for sustained high TPS. Reviewed hosted vs dedicated fallbacks, VPC considerations, and suggested pilot parameters.
topics: long context and KV cache eviction patterns
streaming chunk stalls and client timeouts
sustained high TPS and graceful degradation
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Samira from Redwood, with Diego the SE. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya: Good thanks, running a bit late this morning, appreciate you taking the time.
[00:10] Diego: No worries. Quick agenda — we'll reproduce three customer-vetted edge cases, walk through RCA and remediation patterns in Console and Optimize, and leave 10 minutes for planning a short pilot.
[00:23] Aaron: Cool, just to set context: we're seeing production 2k concurrent sessions, some sessions persist for hours, and occasionally the web client reports stalled streaming — chars stop for 7-15s then resume.
[00:36] Priya: Right, and key constraint: all PHI stays in our VPC, we need audit logs, end-to-end encryption, and low P95 latency — target is 200ms for short queries but willing to accept 600ms for long sessions.
[00:49] Samira: Got it. We'll kick off with a replay of an overlapping-session scenario that triggered KV cache churn. Diego, can you start the demo?
[00:55] Diego: Sure. I'm in the Console — here is the model pool we set up, dedicated-hr-pool. I'll show traffic pattern: bursts of many new long-context sessions and some heavy continuation on a subset. Watch the KV cache metric — it's spiking and evictions climb.
[01:12] Diego: (mouse sounds) So the problem is not CPU but the serving runtime does more random KV cache thrash when many sessions have largely disjoint prefixes. That increases per-token latency.
[01:26] Aaron: Is that the same as our observed P95 blips? We saw token latencies jump from ~180ms to 420ms intermittently.
[01:34] Diego: Yes; it's correlated. Two mitigations: increase per-worker KV cache allocation (memory tradeoff), or change routing so sessions with high shared prefixes are grouped to the same worker (session co-location). Also prefix caching on the client side helps.
[01:50] Priya: Session co-location — is that something Redwood can do automatically?
[01:54] Diego: We have a routing policy in Optimize: you can set a 'sticky-key' selector — hash by conversation id or user id so follow-ups stick to the same worker, reducing eviction. It is available for Dedicated pools; Hosted has soft affinity heuristics.
[02:07] Priya: Ok that helps. Next: the streaming stalls.
[02:11] Diego: Right. I'm going to spin up a simulated client that deliberately drops acks and pauses the TCP read on purpose to emulate slow consuming browsers. Watch the stream timeline.
[02:23] (background console clicks)
[02:26] Diego: See here — the runtime buffers up to N chunks, then backpressure kicks in. If the client stops reading, generate stall; on most browsers the websocket may appear connected but the UI freezes — leading customers to reload and re-open, which creates overlapping sessions.
[02:41] Aaron: Our infra team suspects ephemeral network blips in our mobile clients, which pause reads for ~10s. That matches our incidents.
[02:49] Diego: There are a few levers: 1) streaming chunk-timeout on the server — cut the chunk TTL to drop stale streams sooner, 2) auto-failover to non-streaming longest-available model variant, 3) persistent session handoff — when a stream disconnects we can persist KV cache and allow the next request to resume from alternate worker.
[03:08] Priya: The handoff sounds interesting — but does it leak data between tenants?
[03:12] Samira: Good question — handoff uses encrypted caches in ephemeral storage and KMS keys scoped per-customer in Private or Dedicated. For Hosted we use customer-scoped keys and strict ACLs. We can show audit trails for every handoff event.
[03:27] Maya: From security perspective, we need proof that KV snapshots are zeroized on completion and that KMS CMKs don't leave our control for Private.
[03:34] Samira: We can share the KMS integration doc. For Private we support customer-managed keys and HSMs; handoff snapshots are ephemeral and wiped after TTL and on explicit session termination — we'll link the audit log snippet.
[03:49] Diego: Now the third case: sustained high TPS. I'm pushing 1,200 qps with a mix of short and very long contexts. Console shows queue depth rising and the autoscaler reacting.
[04:00] Diego: See the routing policy — we have latency-tiered routing: premium traffic goes to dedicated workers with lower batch-size and aggressive KV; economy routes to lower-cost quantized variants with higher batch and slightly higher latency.
[04:13] Aaron: We currently prefer hosted for quick scaling. Our worry is: during bursts, the system chooses a cheaper variant and quality drops in sensitive flows. Can we pin a route for a subset of API keys?
[04:25] Samira: Yes, per-route pinning is supported — and you can define fallbacks: prefer model-A but if capacity constrained, fallback to model-A-quantized or to a smaller model; important to tie this to SLOs in Console so alerts fire when fallback occurs.
[04:39] Priya: Can fallback decisions be made regionally? We have EU residency obligations.
[04:44] Diego: Absolutely; routing policy is region-aware. We'll route EU keys only to EU capacity; if EU is saturated we can fail closed or direct to a dedicated reserve in EU.
[04:55] Priya: Another question — streaming timeouts: what are recommended client-side keepalive parameters?
[05:00] Diego: We recommend a client read timeout slightly longer than server chunk-ttl, e.g., chunk-ttl 8s, client read 12s, and websocket pings every 10s. That reduces false positives but allows the server to drop truly dead streams.
[05:14] Aaron: For our mobile SDK, we can implement that. But one more thing — the handoff: how long does a persisted KV snapshot live?
[05:21] Diego: Default TTL is 10 minutes, configurable per-pool. For HIPAA customers we often drop to 2 minutes unless a legal hold is needed.
[05:30] Priya: Can we audit how often handoff occurs? We want to correlate with client crash reports.
[05:35] Samira: Yes, audit logs show handoff events with session id, worker id, reason code, timestamp. You can ship these to your SIEM or view in Console.
[05:45] (background keyboard)
[05:48] Diego: I'm switching to Optimize — we have a runbook here that suggested increasing worker mem, setting sticky-key to user-id, and enabling chunk-ttl at 8s. I'm applying these to a staging dedicated pool now.
[06:02] Priya: Will that change require restarts?
[06:06] Diego: No live restart; many routing and policy changes are dynamic. Increasing per-worker mem may require node replacement for dedicated on-prem setups.
[06:13] Aaron: Ok so practically we run a short pilot — what metrics should we watch?
[06:17] Diego: Watch avg KV evictions, per-token latency p95, streaming chunk backlog, and handoff frequency. We'll provide a spreadsheet with expected thresholds.
[06:26] Priya: Great. Security: Maya — anything else?
[06:29] Maya: Just one ask — we need a SOC2 audit statement and confirmation on data residency for Dedicated in our VPC.
[06:35] Samira: We'll share the SOC2 cert and a Private deployment architecture note for VPC peering + KMS flow.
[06:41] (brief pause)
[06:45] Diego: Demo wrap: reproduced KV thrash, demonstrated streaming stall mechanics, showed routing/fallback and handoff.
[06:52] Priya: Helpful. A few nitpicks — can we limit routing changes to a subset of keys for controlled rollout?
[06:57] Samira: Yes, Canary route can be applied to a percentage of API keys; Console shows per-key metrics.
[07:03] Aaron: And pricing — dedicated pool with pinned routing, do you have an estimate for our 2k concurrent session profile?
[07:10] Samira: I'll send a tailored estimate; the baseline is monthly committed capacity plus per-token. We have a cost-sensitivity dashboard in Console to show unit economics if you want to iterate.
[07:22] Priya: Timeline — we want a 2-week pilot, then decision. Can Redwood support a 48–72h soak first?
[07:29] Samira: Yes, 48–72h dedicated short pilot is our standard. We'll provision a small dedicated pool and capture metrics.
[07:35] Maya: One security clarification — during pilot will audit logs be streamed to our logging endpoint?
[07:40] Diego: Yes, we can forward logs to your SIEM via secure syslog or cloud log connector for the pilot.
[07:47] Priya: Thanks.
[07:49] Samira: OK next steps we'll recap in a moment. Any last questions?
[07:53] Aaron: One more — in the case of massive KV churn, is there a recommended client pattern to reduce replays?
[07:59] Diego: Yes: compact prompts before sending (strip redundant prefixes), keep smaller incremental deltas, and where possible offload stable context to embeddings and pass pointers.
[08:11] Priya: Good catch.
[08:13] Samira: Alright we'll close the demo and summarize actions.
[08:17] (wrap-up chatter)
[08:21] Samira: Thanks everyone, we'll email the pilot plan, KB links, pricing, and security docs.
[08:27] Priya: Thanks Samira, Diego.
[08:29] Maya: Thanks.
[08:30] Samira: Bye.
